history.heading: Medieval Serbia
paragraphs: Slavs settled the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries. Serbian principalities emerged, and in the 12th century Stefan Nemanja founded the Nemanjić dynasty. His son, Saint Sava, established the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church in 1219. Under Stefan Dušan, crowned emperor in 1346, Serbia became one of the most powerful states in the Balkans.
The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 against the Ottomans became a central part of Serbian national identity. Serbia fell fully under Ottoman rule by 1459.

history.heading: Uprisings and independence
paragraphs: The First and Second Serbian Uprisings (1804 and 1815) led to an autonomous principality. Serbia gained full independence in 1878 and became a kingdom in 1882. It expanded in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by a Bosnian Serb in 1914 triggered the First World War, in which Serbia lost a large share of its population. In 1918 it became the core of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia.

history.heading: Yugoslavia and its breakup
paragraphs: During the Second World War, Serbia was occupied by Germany, and both royalist Chetniks and communist Partisans resisted. Belgrade was the capital of socialist Yugoslavia under Tito.

In the 1990s, under Slobodan Milošević, Yugoslavia's breakup led to wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. NATO bombed Serbia in 1999. Milošević was overthrown in 2000 and tried for war crimes. Montenegro separated in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise. In 2024–25, after a railway station canopy collapse in Novi Sad killed 16 people, student-led mass protests against corruption swept the country.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts. Most Serbs are Orthodox Christians, and the slava, a family's patron saint day, is recognised by UNESCO. Medieval monasteries such as Studenica are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Inventor Nikola Tesla, of Serbian origin, is a national icon, and Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Filmmaker Emir Kusturica and the Guča trumpet festival are well known.

culture.heading: Food and sport
paragraphs: Serbian food includes ćevapi, pljeskavica (grilled meat patties), sarma and ajvar, with rakija (fruit brandy). Serbia excels in sport: tennis star Novak Djokovic, basketball (Nikola Jokić), water polo and volleyball.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Serbia is a parliamentary republic. Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party have dominated politics since 2012; critics accuse the government of restricting media freedom and weakening institutions. The 2024–25 protests led to the prime minister's resignation.
Serbia is an EU candidate country but maintains close ties with Russia and China and has not joined sanctions against Russia. It is militarily neutral.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Serbia has an upper-middle-income economy. Key sectors include manufacturing (cars, tyres and electronics, with Chinese and European investment), agriculture (raspberries, maize and wheat), mining (copper and gold), IT and services. A large lithium deposit in the Jadar valley is controversial due to environmental concerns.
The currency is the dinar. Belgrade is hosting Expo 2027.
